did_you_know.text: Habakkuk opens with the words, “The oracle that he saw,” presenting the prophet’s message as a vision or a prophetic burden that he bears.
Habakkuk repeatedly cries out to the Lord about violence, yet describes feeling that his cry goes unanswered: “How long… and you do not listen?”
The prophet describes a situation in which the law is weakened, justice is not carried out properly, and the wicked surround the righteous; therefore, justice is perverted.
In his reply, the Lord directs attention to the nations and announces that he is carrying out an act in the prophet’s days that would be difficult to believe if it were told.
The people whom the Lord is raising up are the Chaldeans, described as a bitter and swift nation that sweeps across the earth to seize dwellings that do not belong to them.

The speed of the Chaldean army is described through images from the animal world: their horses are swifter than leopards, and their horsemen are like evening wolves and an eagle swooping down to devour.
The Chaldeans mock kings and rulers, and even fortresses do not deter them; they pile up earth and capture the city.
After describing the conqueror’s power, the passage says that he moves on and sins because he attributes his strength to his god: “This is his power; it is his god.”
Habakkuk emphasizes the moral difficulty of the situation: how can the Lord, whose eyes are too pure to look at evil, allow the wicked to swallow up someone more righteous than himself?
The conqueror is described as a fisherman who catches people with a hook, a net, and a dragnet; this image emphasizes the capture of nations and the joy taken in the spoils.
